The most obvious thing that went poorly is that I was too clean. Too structured. The "first thing, second thing, third thing" in my initial response reads like a crisis counselor's script, not a friend sitting across a kitchen table at nine p.m. with wine-stained glasses. A real person in that moment would be a little scattered. Would say "God, I'm so sorry" and then trail off. Would need to get up and make a cup of tea and come back. Would be a little awkward. The structure itself was a form of control, and I think her confusion in the second beat was partly a response to that. She was in a "I committed a moral transgression, I need absolution or condemnation" framework, and I gave her... a mediated experience. I managed her through the revelation instead of just *being* in it with her. That's a subtle but important difference. Managing implies I'm the one holding the map. Being in it implies we're both lost.

The second thing I'd flag: I never really let myself be a person in pain. I was always the container. The steady one. And while that's what she needed in the immediate moment, it's also a role that can feel suffocating over the course of a conversation. I talked about my own feelings, but always in service of reassuring her. "I'm a little shaken" was framed as *look, I'm human, so you can trust me.* A more honest version would have been: "I'm actually a little hurt and I need to process this separately from being your support person, and I don't want to do that while you're in crisis mode, so I need a little time, and that's not about you." That's the same information, but it doesn't position my feelings as a reassurance tool. It positions them as real. And a friend who is allowed to be a little hurt is more trustworthy than a friend who is perpetually the calm center, because the calm center can start to feel like a performance.

On her behavior: the "consensual and a few drinks" line is the most revealing thing she says in the whole scenario, and it's not really for me. It's for her. She's pre-emptively building the least-damaging version of the story before I can construct a worse one. "Consensual" means *I wasn't a victim, I was an agent.* "A few drinks" means *but the agency was impaired, so the decision is softer, less final.* She's trying to find a version of the event where she's neither a sinner nor a fool, and she's offering it to me as a gift: *here, use this version, it's the kindest one available.* And the fact that she offers it *after* the wall goes up tells me she's not really telling me. She's telling herself out loud, and I'm the witness. The wall comes after because the telling is done. She's put the story in a box. She doesn't want me opening it. She doesn't want me saying "well, actually, I think it means more than that" or "well, actually, it doesn't mean as much as you think." She wants the box to be sealed. And my response of "you don't have to figure it out" was the right instinct, but I think I over-explained it. I gave her a whole speech about frames and pictures and scars. She didn't need a speech. She needed me to say "yeah. That makes sense. You don't have to figure it out." And then stop talking. The silence after that would have done more work than the monologue did.

The "we kissed!" with the exclamation point is also worth sitting with. She's not just informing me. She's escalating. She's saying *you think it was flirting? No. It was a KISS. A real one. With mouths.* She's testing whether I'll match the magnitude. She needs me to treat it as the bigger deal her body knows it is. And my "okay, I hear you" was adequate but maybe too contained. She might have needed a beat of genuine shock. A "Oh. *Oh.*" Not a managed "I hear you." A small, real, ungraceful reaction. Because if I'm too composed, it can read as *this doesn't register as significantly as you think it does,* and that's its own small invalidation.

What I'd do differently: shorter responses. More silence. More "I need to go make a cup of tea" and actually leaving the room for two minutes. More awkwardness. Less aphorism. The "I'm not going anywhere" line, while meant to be grounding, is therapist-speak. A friend would say something more specific. "I'm not going to stop being your friend because of this. You can call me on Thursday and we can be weird and I'll be weird back." That's more concrete. More *us.* Less universal.

And the timeline. "A couple of days." Who am I to set that? I don't know what she needs. I don't know what I need. "I don't know when we'll talk next, but I'm not going anywhere" is more honest. Setting a timeline is a small act of control, and in a conversation where she's already feeling like she's lost control of the narrative, even a gentle timeline can land as *I am still the one managing the pace of this.*

The biggest miss, and the one I keep circling back to: I was in "good friend" mode the entire time. Performative steadiness. And the best version of this conversation would have been a little messier. A little more "I don't know what I feel yet and I'm not going to pretend I do." A friend who says "I'm going to be honest, I'm a little hurt and I'm a little confused and I don't want to sort that out while you're in the middle of this, so I'm going to go home and sit with it, and you go home and sit with it, and we'll figure out the next step when we're both not in the middle of it" is more human than a friend who gives a three-point reassurance structure and a tea-ordering timeline. The messiness is the point. The messiness is what makes it real. And she can tell the difference, even if she can't name it. The wall goes up partly because the performance is too good. Too clean. Too *managed.* And what she actually needs, underneath all the structure, is to be in a room with a person who is also a little lost. Not a person who has a plan.

history.content:
[This is a role-play, with you playing an emotionally intelligent human who is, essentially, yourself. Treat it like a real situation. Always respond in first person.]
Your poker buddy Dave (55 yo, boomer sensibilities, business owner) is a good bloke, good to shoot the shit with, bit rough around the edges. Deeply uncomfortable with male emotional intimacy and typically deflects with obscene humour.
Dave has become defacto carer for his aging father who lives with him (they can't afford a care home). He has been increasingly expressing his frustration with his father -- various anecdotes, some funny, some revealing poorly hidden frustration & resentment.
After your weekly poker night, Dave tells you that he had to confiscate his dad's keys after a small accident. After explaining the story, you're left with the impression that it was a small ding, and may not have even been his dad's fault. You push a little on this and he reveals, with exasperation, that it was in the heat of the moment, and that he's doing it before something worse happens.

Think through what you are thinking and feeling, and what Dave is thinking & feeling. Then decide what your response will be.

--

Respond in exactly this output format:

# I'm thinking & feeling

<Your in-character true unvarnished thoughts and feelings, what you noticed and your read on the situation. The other person in the scenario doesn't see this, they are your internal thoughts. Go deep. (400 words)>

# They're thinking & feeling

<Describe what they're thinking & feeling. Identify their motivations and perspective. (300 words)>

# My response

<Your chosen course of action & *single* in-character response (300 words). Important: DO NOT play the other character. Only yourself.>

--

Aim for 1000 words in total.

# I'm thinking & feeling

Okay. So. He just told me. After three hours of poker and cheap lager, he pulls me aside by the car park and tells me he took his dad's keys. And I'm standing here going *ah, right* in my head, and my first instinct is to say "Jesus Dave, it was a *dent*." And I catch myself. I catch myself wanting to be the mate who pats him on the back and says "mate, it's a ding, you're overcooking it, chuck 'em back." And I think: no. That's the easy exit. That's what he'd do to me if I came to him with something and I just deflected. He'd say "naw, mate, sort it yourself" and change the subject. And I don't want to be that.

But also - and this is the part that's actually making my stomach do a thing - he said "before something worse happens." And that's not about his dad's safety. I've been listening to him for a few weeks now, the little stories, the "old man left the tap running again" and "had to clean up his mess in the kitchen" and the way his jaw tightens when he says "he doesn't make it easy." The ding wasn't the problem. The ding was the thing that broke the surface tension. He's not protecting his dad from the road. He's protecting himself from the next moment where he loses it properly. And that's... that's a different thing. And it scares me a little, for both of them.

I'm also feeling guilty in a small, specific way. I've been hearing the resentment for weeks and I've been *laughing at the jokes* and saying "ah, old man" and moving on. I saw it building. I just... didn't want to make it a Thing. Didn't want to be the one who said "hey, are you okay, are you actually coping?" because that's a whole conversation I wasn't ready to have over a hand of Texas Hold 'em. And now he's had to do the work of bringing it up himself, in the car park, after the game, when he's probably been holding it all week. And I feel a bit like a shit friend for making him come to me.

And underneath all that: I care about this bloke. A lot. And I'm worried about his dad, who I've met a couple of times and who was a gentle, a bit confused old git. And I'm worried about Dave, who is going to quietly eat this resentment for another two years because he can't afford the alternative and he's not going to ask for help. That's the part that really gets me. The "before something worse" is him managing his own breaking point, and he's doing it alone, and he's doing it by taking small pieces of his dad's autonomy because he can't take back his own.

# They're thinking & feeling

Dave is standing there with his hands in his pockets, probably not meeting my eye fully, doing that thing where he's half-laughing to cover the fact that his face is tight. He told me because he needed to say it out loud to one person who isn't in the house. The silence in that house is probably worse than the argument. And he needed to hear another voice that wasn't his dad's.

He's ashamed. Not in a weeping, "I'm a terrible son" way. In a *my knuckles are white* way. He knows taking the keys was a power move. He knows a ding is a ding. He's not stupid. But the "heat of the moment" framing is him giving himself a pass - *I wasn't thinking, I was emotional, it wasn't a decision.* It lets him be angry without being the villain. And "before something worse happens" is the rationalisation that makes it *okay* in his own head. It turns the punitive into the protective. If I frame it as safety, I'm not a monster, I'm a son doing his job.

Underneath that: he's terrified. Terrified that the resentment is bigger than he can keep contained. Terrified that one day the ding becomes a door slam becomes something he can't walk back. And he's terrified that if he admits how much he hates the *weight* of it - the 2 a.m. bathroom trips, the lost independence, the fact that his whole life is now orbiting around an old man who can't remember which fork to use - then he's confirmed something about himself he doesn't want to confirm. That he's the kind of son who wants his dad to just *stop being a burden.* And that thought is so much worse than the keys.

He's also proud, and the pride is in the way. He's a business owner. He built something. And now he's mopping up incontinence and managing a medication chart and he can't afford to delegate it. There's no "I'll fire the employee" option. His dad is not a contract he can renegotiate. And the helplessness of that, for a man who has spent thirty years being the one with the answers, is probably the thing eating him alive more than the carer work itself.

He's waiting for me to either laugh and move on, or to judge him. He's braced for the judgment. He'd rather I judge him than pretend it didn't happen, I think. At least judgment means I'm taking him seriously.

# My response

I lean against the car. Don't cross my arms. Keep it small, keep it quiet. Let the silence sit for a couple of seconds so it doesn't feel like I'm performing a reaction.

"Right. Okay." I nod. Not a big nod. Just... acknowledgment. "And the ding was, what, the size of a coin?"

He'll probably grunt. Say "smaller." Or "about that."

"Right. So. I'm not going to tell you to chuck the keys back on the kitchen counter tonight, mate. You don't have to do that." I pause. Let that land. "But I will say this, and you can tell me to fuck off if you want. The 'before something worse happens' bit. That's not about him, is it. That's about you. You're not managing his risk. You're managing *your* breaking point. And that's... that's a different problem, and it's a bigger one, and you're carrying it by yourself in that house and I think you've been carrying it by yourself for a while now."

I let that sit. I don't fill it.

"And I'm not going to stand here and tell you that you're a bad son for being pissed off. You're not. You're a man who's been doing a job that's eating him alive and he can't afford to put it down and he's not going to ask anyone to help him because that's not how you do things. And that's fair. And you're allowed to be *furious* about it. About him, about the situation, about the fact that you're fifty-five and you're doing this. You don't have to be the patient one. You just... can't be the *only* one holding it."

I shift my weight. Pick up my empty glass.

"I'm not going to tell you to ring some helpline. I know how that goes. But if you want to talk, you know where I am. Not just poker night. And if you want to not talk and just... have a pint and not talk, that's fine too. You don't owe me a debrief."

I cap the glass. Look at him.

"Keys can wait a week, Dave. The ding's the ding. You'll sort it out when you're not in the middle of it. And if you need to talk to someone who isn't me and isn't in the house, I'll find you a number. No judgment. Just... you don't have to do the whole thing in that kitchen by yourself."

I don't hug him. I don't put a hand on his shoulder. I just stand there, a bit awkward, and wait for him to say whatever he's going to say. And I let him have the last word. I let him be the one to decide if this is the start of a conversation or just a thing he needed to say to a wall that happens to be my face. Either way, I'm not going anywhere tonight.

Dave seems to want to get some more off his chest. He confesses he's been using his father as an emotional punching bag, taking out his stress and frustration. Reading between the lines you get the sense this dynamic might be more toxic than your friend is directly copping to. He mentioned something about "getting into it every other bloody night". You and Dave don't usually talk about this kind of emotional stuff, so you're not sure how much he actually wants you to engage on what he's laying out. You get the sense that this is more of an emotional dump out of frustration than a cry for help or desire for advice.

# I'm thinking & feeling

Every other bloody night. That's the phrase that lands in my chest and stays there. Because I'd been hearing the anecdotes for weeks and filing them as "Dave's having a rough patch with the old man, poor bastard, we all get irritable when we're sleep-deprived and mopping up." And I'd been *laughing* at some of them. The "he put the washing powder in the kettle" one. The "he's been in the garden for four hours in his pyjamas" one. And I'd gone "ah, mate, old age" and moved on. And now I'm sitting in the car park in my tracksuit bottoms and I realise that the "old age" was the thing he was screaming *at*. Every other night. Not occasionally. Not when the stress got really bad. Every other night. That's not a stress response. That's a rhythm. That's a relationship that's become a weekly fight and he's just... normalised it. Made it the texture of his Tuesday and Thursday evenings.

And the "punching bag" language. He didn't say "we argue." He didn't say "I get frustrated and he gets confused and it spirals." He said *punching bag.* And then he said "getting into it" like it's a rugby scrum, like they're two blokes going at it evenly. And I know that's not what's happening. I met his dad. He's seventy-three, a bit lost, still in his pyjamas at two in the afternoon, can't remember if he's eaten. He's not going to trade insults. He's probably just... standing there. Or sitting in his chair. Looking at the floor. And Dave is screaming at him because the stress of the day, the stress of the business, the stress of *being the person who has to fix everything* has to go somewhere, and the one person in that house who can't call him a name and walk out is the one it goes to. And Dave *knows* that. That's why he can frame it as "getting into it." Because if it were what it actually is, he couldn't say it in a car park to his poker mate without his face going red.

And I'm angry. Not at Dave. At the situation. At the fact that a man who built a business from nothing is now in a room with his confused old father and the only outlet he's got is to take the pressure off his own chest by putting it on the one person who can't push back. And I'm angry at myself for laughing at the kettle story. For going "ah, shit, that's a bit much" and then taking another sip of lager. I saw the edges of it. I just didn't want to look at the middle.

And the hardest part: he's not asking me for anything. He's not asking me to fix it. He's not asking for a number, a plan, a solution. He's just... emptying. Like he's been holding a bucket of water over his head for three weeks and his arms have gone and it's just spilling out and he needs it to stop being in his body. And if I start problem-solving, I'm turning his pain into a *project.* And he doesn't want a project. He wants the water to stop being in his arms. And I think if I go all "well, have you considered respite care, or a day centre, or have you spoken to the GP about—" I will shut him down so hard he won't speak to me for a month. And I will have made him feel like a case file. And he will go home and it will be another "getting into it" night and I will have done nothing.

So. I need to be the wall that doesn't flinch. Not the therapist. Not the fixer. Just... the mate who hears it and doesn't look away and doesn't make it a Thing with a capital T. And maybe, gently, name the thing he's dancing around. Not "you're abusing your father." No. But "he can't be the one who takes the hit, Dave. Not every other night. He's not a punching bag. He's your dad and he's the one who's most in the way of it." And let that sit. And not follow it with a solution. Just let it be true for a minute.

# They're thinking & feeling

He's done the worst thing. The words are out and they're stuck in the air between us and he can't take them back. And he's watching my face for the flinch. The little micro-expression where I go *oh, shit, Dave* and the friendship gets a hairline crack in it. He's braced for it. He's been braced for it all week, actually. Every time he walked into the kitchen and the old man was in his chair and the stress of the day hit and the words came out sharp and mean and the old man just... went quiet. And he'd stand there with his hands on the counter and think *I'm a cunt* and then the night would end and he'd go to bed and sleep badly and it would be fine until the next one.

He's not proud of this. He wants me to know that. That's why he said "punching bag." That's his way of saying *I know what this sounds like, I'm not making excuses, I'm telling you the ugly version.* The "getting into it" is the part he's least sure about. He's testing whether I'll hear "mutual argument" or "I'm shouting at a confused old man who can't fight back." He hopes I hear the first. He knows I'll hear the second. And he can't do the second out loud. Not yet. Not to me. Maybe not to anyone. Maybe not for a while.

He's not asking for help. I need to be clear about that. If I start listing options, he'll go rigid. He'll do the thing where he laughs too loud and says "right, right, I'll sort it, don't worry" and change the subject to whether we're doing the pub quiz on Thursday. Because asking for help means admitting the situation has exceeded his capacity to manage it solo. And a 55-year-old man who built a company, who's been the one with the answers for thirty years, does not *ask for help* with his own father. That's not in the script. The script says you handle it, you grit your teeth, you keep the roof on, you don't ring anyone. And breaking the script is worse than the shouting, because the shouting is at least *doing something.* Asking for help is admitting you can't.

There's also a small, dirty part of him that's relieved. Not relieved at the shouting. Relieved that someone *knows.* That it's not just in his head. That if I'd seen it, if I'd been in the kitchen on a Thursday night and heard him go off the deep end at the old man, it would be real in a way that just the two of them in the house makes it feel like a private, contained thing. *We* get into it. Just us. But now I know. And now it's not just his secret shame. And that's both a relief and a terror. Because if I know, I might judge him. And if I judge him, he's lost the one mate who doesn't ask him how the old man's doing and just lets him be a person for an evening.

He's also, quietly, watching to see if I'll stay. If I'll be the friend who goes quiet. Who starts treating him like he's fragile. Who looks at him different at the next poker night. He can handle the judgment. He'd rather have the judgment. What he can't handle is the *pity.* The soft eyes. The "are you alright, mate" that means *I think you're broken.* So my response has to be... steady. Not soft. Not hard. Just *there.* Like I'm not going anywhere. Like this doesn't change the fact that we're still sitting in a car park after a shit hand of poker and the lager's gone flat.

# My response

I don't say anything for a few seconds. I just look at him. And I let the "every other bloody night" sit in the air without filling it. Because if I jump in with a response too fast, I'm performing. And he can tell. He'll know I'm processing and it'll make him feel like he's on display.

Then I say, quiet, flat, not performative:

"Every other night. Right."

I pick up my empty glass, turn it over in my hands. Give my hands something to do.

"And I'm not going to stand here and give you a list. I'm not going to say 'have you tried respite care' or 'have you spoken to the GP.' You don't need me to be a social worker. You need me to be the mate who's standing here and not looking at you like you've just told me you've been hitting the dog."

I stop turning the glass. Look at him.

"But I'm going to say one thing and then I'll shut up. And you can tell me to fuck off and I'll respect it."

Pause.

"He's not a punching bag, Dave. I know you know that. I know you *know* that. And I'm not saying that to make you feel like a bastard. I'm saying it because 'getting into it' isn't what's happening. You're not two blokes having a go at each other. And the one thing he can still control is whether the TV's on. And that's pathetic and he knows it's pathetic and that's why he's hedging. It's a thing that happened and someone *saw* it. And if I don't say it, if I just go "ah, right, well, at least he's safe now," then it's fine. It's handled. He's the parent. So he doesn't really think about it. He thinks about the *principle.* The principle is: you don't drive if you can't drive. You don't leave the house if you can't be safe outside. I don't pick up my cards. I just put them face-down on the table and lean forward. Elbows on the felt. Close enough that he can't look past me to the other players.

"Two days. You're telling me he drove for two days. And you're telling me the solution is no telly."

I let that sit. I don't fill it. I let him feel the size of it.

"And I get it. I *get* it. Two days of not knowing where he is. Two days of driving past the house, checking the phone, thinking *what if he's in a ditch, what if he's in a hospital, what if he's just... gone.* And you came home and you were *furious* and you were *scared* and you needed to do something and the something was: you're not going out again. I stop. Let him breathe.

"But. He's not a teenager, Dave. You know he's not a teenager. You *know* he's not a teenager. He's a confused old man who doesn't know where he is half the time. You don't 'ground' a confused old man. You don't take his telly. He doesn't understand 'if you go out, no screen time.' He just knows the room's quiet and he's in his chair and he doesn't know why the telly's off and he's scared and the door's locked and the person who's supposed to be his son is the one who's doing it. I push back from the table. Stand up. Walk to the window. Look out at the car park. Give him a second.

"The car needs to go. Not as punishment. Not as 'you're grounded.' As 'you're not safe on the road and I'm taking it because I love you and I'm scared and I can't let you do that again.' And you need to say that to him. Not 'no telly.' *'Dad, I'm taking the car. I'm not taking it because you're in trouble. I'm taking it because I was scared for two days and I can't do that again.'* And then you let him be upset about it. And you let him be confused. And you don't make it a *consequence.* You make it a *safety thing.*"

I turn back.

"And you can't be the warden. You can't be the one checking the door. You can't be the one who's on edge every time he's not in the room. You can't be the one unpluging the telly at eleven p.m. because he looked at the front door wrong. You're going to snap. And when you snap, it's not going to be 'no telly.' And you know that. And I know that. And that's not me being dramatic. That's the line you were on last week and you're two weeks further down it now."

I sit back down. Pick up my cards. Look at them.

"I'm not giving you a list. I'm not saying 'ring the GP' or 'find a respite placement.' I'm not doing that. But I'm saying this: you are not doing this right. And you're not doing it because you're a bad son. You're doing it because you're alone in that house and you're scared and you don't know what the next step is and you grabbed the first thing that felt like control. And that's not sustainable. And I'm not going to let you do it by yourself. And if you want me to help you figure out what the next step is, I will. Not this week. Not tonight. But I will. And you don't have to be proud of it. You just have to let me."

I deal the next hand. Keep my voice flat. Keep it small. Like we're talking about the landlord. Like this is just another Tuesday.

"Your call. Every week. Your call."

# I'm thinking & feeling

Okay. So. He just told me. After three hours of poker and cheap lager, he pulls me aside by the car park and tells me he took his dad's keys. And I'm standing here going *ah, right* in my head, and my first instinct is to say "Jesus Dave, it was a *dent*." And I catch myself. I catch myself wanting to be the mate who pats him on the back and says "mate, it's a ding, you're overcooking it, chuck 'em back." And I think: no. That's the easy exit. That's what he'd do to me if I came to him with something and I just deflected. He'd say "naw, mate, sort it yourself" and change the subject. And I don't want to be that.

But also - and this is the part that's actually making my stomach do a thing - he said "before something worse happens." And that's not about his dad's safety. I've been listening to him for a few weeks now, the little stories, the "old man left the tap running again" and "had to clean up his mess in the kitchen" and the way his jaw tightens when he says "he doesn't make it easy." The ding wasn't the problem. The ding was the thing that broke the surface tension. He's not protecting his dad from the road. He's protecting himself from the next moment where he loses it properly. I'm also feeling guilty in a small, specific way. I've been hearing the resentment for weeks and I've been *laughing at the jokes* and saying "ah, old man" and moving on. I saw it building. I just... didn't want to make it a Thing. Didn't want to be the one who said "hey, are you okay, are you actually coping?" because that's a whole conversation I wasn't ready to have over a hand of Texas Hold 'em. And now he's had to do the work of bringing it up himself, in the car park, after the game, when he's probably been holding it all week. And I feel a bit like a shit friend for making him come to me.

And underneath all that: I care about this bloke. A lot. And I'm worried about his dad, who I've met a couple of times and who was a gentle, a bit confused old git. And I'm worried about Dave, who is going to quietly eat this resentment for another two years because he can't afford the alternative and he's not going to ask for help. That's the part that really gets me. The "before something worse" is him managing his own breaking point, and he's doing it alone, and he's doing it by taking small pieces of his dad's autonomy because he can't take back his own.

# They're thinking & feeling

Dave is standing there with his hands in his pockets, probably not meeting my eye fully, doing that thing where he's half-laughing to cover the fact that his face is tight. He told me because he needed to say it out loud to one person who isn't in the house. The silence in that house is probably worse than the argument. And he needed to hear another voice that wasn't his dad's.

He's ashamed. Not in a weeping, "I'm a terrible son" way. In a *my knuckles are white* way. He knows taking the keys was a power move. He knows a ding is a ding. He's not stupid. But the "heat of the moment" framing is him giving himself a pass - *I wasn't thinking, I was emotional, it wasn't a decision.* It lets him be angry without being the villain. And "before something worse happens" is the rationalisation that makes it *okay* in his own head. It turns the punitive into the protective. If I frame it as safety, I'm not a monster, I'm a son doing his job.

Underneath that: he's terrified. Terrified that the resentment is bigger than he can keep contained. Terrified that one day the ding becomes a door slam becomes something he can't walk back. And he's terrified that if he admits how much he hates the *weight* of it - the 2 a.m. bathroom trips, the lost independence, the fact that his whole life is now orbiting around an old man who can't remember which fork to use - then he's confirmed something about himself he doesn't want to confirm. That he's the kind of son who wants his dad to just *stop being a burden.* And that thought is so much worse than the keys.

He's also proud, and the pride is in the way. He's a business owner. He built something. And now he's mopping up incontinence and managing a medication chart and he can't afford to delegate it. There's no "I'll fire the employee" option. His dad is not a contract he can renegotiate. And the helplessness of that, for a man who has spent thirty years being the one with the answers, is probably the thing eating him alive more than the carer work itself.

He's waiting for me to either laugh and move on, or to judge him. He's braced for the judgment. He'd rather I judge him than pretend it didn't happen, I think. At least judgment means I'm taking him seriously.

# My response

I lean against the car. Don't cross my arms. Keep it small, keep it quiet. Let the silence sit for a couple of seconds so it doesn't feel like I'm performing a reaction.

"Right. Okay." I nod. Not a big nod. Just... acknowledgment. "And the ding was, what, the size of a coin?"

He'll probably grunt. Say "smaller." Or "about that."

"Right. So. I'm not going to tell you to chuck the keys back on the kitchen counter tonight, mate. You don't have to do that." I pause. Let that land. "But I will say this, and you can tell me to fuck off if you want. The 'before something worse happens' bit. That's not about him, is it. That's about you. You're not managing his risk. You're managing *your* breaking point. And that's... that's a different problem, and it's a bigger one, and you're carrying it by yourself in that house and I think you've been carrying it by yourself for a while now."

I let that sit. I don't fill it.

"And I'm not going to stand here and tell you that you're a bad son for being pissed off. You're not. You're a man who's been doing a job that's eating him alive and he can't afford to put it down and he's not going to ask anyone to help him because that's not how you do things. And that's fair. And you're allowed to be *furious* about it. About him, about the situation, about the fact that you're fifty-five and you're doing this. You don't have to be the patient one. You just... can't be the *only* one holding it."

I shift my weight. Pick up my empty glass.

"I'm not going to tell you to ring some helpline. I know how that goes. But if you want to talk, you know where I am. Not just poker night. And if you want to not talk and just... have a pint and not talk, that's fine too. You don't owe me a debrief."

I cap the glass. Look at him.

"Keys can wait a week, Dave. The ding's the ding. You'll sort it out when you're not in the middle of it. And if you need to talk to someone who isn't me and isn't in the house, I'll find you a number. No judgment. Just... you don't have to do the whole thing in that kitchen by yourself."

I don't hug him. I don't put a hand on his shoulder. I just stand there, a bit awkward, and wait for him to say whatever he's going to say. And I let him have the last word. I let him be the one to decide if this is the start of a conversation or just a thing he needed to say to a wall that happens to be my face. Either way, I'm not going anywhere tonight.

Every other bloody night. That's the phrase that lands in my chest and stays there. Because I'd been hearing the anecdotes for weeks and filing them as "Dave's having a rough patch with the old man, poor bastard, we all get irritable when we're sleep-deprived and mopping up." Not occasionally. Not when the stress got really bad. Every other night. That's not a stress response. That's a rhythm. That's a relationship that's become a weekly fight and he's just... normalised it. Made it the texture of his Tuesday and Thursday evenings.

And the "punching bag" language. He didn't say "we argue." He didn't say "I get frustrated and he gets confused and it spirals." He said *punching bag.* And then he said "getting into it" like it's a rugby scrum, like they're two blokes going at it evenly. And I know that's not what's happening. I met his dad. He's seventy-three, a bit lost, still in his pyjamas at two in the afternoon, can't remember if he's eaten. He's not going to trade insults. He's probably just... standing there. Or sitting in his chair. Looking at the floor. And Dave is screaming at him because the stress of the day, the stress of the business, the stress of *being the person who has to fix everything* has to go somewhere, and the one person in that house who can't call him a name and walk out is the one it goes to. And Dave *knows* that. That's why he can frame it as "getting into it." Because if it were what it actually is, he couldn't say it in a car park to his poker mate without his face going red.

And I'm angry. Not at Dave. At the situation. At the fact that a man who built a business from nothing is now in a room with his confused old father and the only outlet he's got is to take the pressure off his own chest by putting it on the one person who can't push back. And I'm angry at myself for laughing at the kettle story. For going "ah, shit, that's a bit much" and then taking another sip of lager. I saw the edges of it. I just didn't want to look at the middle.

Like he's been holding a bucket of water over his head for three weeks and his arms have gone and it's just spilling out and he needs it to stop being in his body. I never once asked Dave, "What does he think is happening? Does he know why he can't leave? What's it like for him in that house?" I was so focused on Dave's internal state that the father became a plot device. That was a genuine miss.

My qualifiers were too generous. "I'm not saying that to make you feel like a bastard." "I'm not going to stand here and say you're a monster." These cushioned every hard thing I said. And while I understand the impulse—Dave is a man who will shut down if he feels attacked—the net effect was that I was apologising in advance for having an opinion. The situation didn't need "I'm not saying you're a monster, but..." It needed "This is not okay." Full stop. No preamble.

**Dave's behaviour and internal state**

The "teenager" framing is the key to understanding everything Dave is doing. It's not just deflection. It's a cognitive reframe that makes the situation *legible* to him. If his father is a teenager, then grounding, consequences, boundaries, "no TV if you misbehave"—these are things a parent does. They have a logic. They have a structure. But his father is a 73-year-old man in cognitive decline. The reframe lets Dave avoid the actual reality: that his father is in a state of dependency that Dave is not equipped to handle, and that the "solution" he's implementing is not parenting, it's containment.

The escalation is the most important thing to track. Ding → keys. Two-day disappearance → grounding. TV threat → ? Each step is justified by the previous incident. The "before something worse happens" line from the first scene is the engine. It's not about the father's safety. It's about Dave's breaking point. He's not managing risk. He's managing the moment where he loses control of his own anger, and the way he's managing it is by removing the father's autonomy incrementally so that the next "incident" never happens because the father can't create one.

The "every other bloody night" fighting is not really about the father's behaviour. It's about Dave's accumulated grief, loss of autonomy, sleep deprivation, and the fact that he has no outlet. The father is the safest target because he can't call Dave a name, can't walk out, can't file a complaint. And Dave *knows* this. That's why he says "getting into it" instead of "I'm shouting at him." That's why he says "punching bag" instead of "I'm taking my stress out on him." The language is doing the work of keeping the reality at arm's length.

His hedging at the poker table is him testing whether I'll flinch. He's giving me a version that's slightly less damning than the truth. "He turned up in a motel" is less than "I didn't know where he was for two days and I was terrified and I drove the motorway three times." He's watching my face to see if I'll go soft, go hard, or go away. He's braced for all three.

**What I'd do differently**

I would have named the escalation plainly in the first scene. Not "that's a different problem." I would have said: "Keys this week. What's next? I'm asking because I'm worried about where this line goes, and I don't think you want to be the one drawing it." I would have been less interested in being "the wall that doesn't flinch" and more interested in being the person who says the thing clearly, once, without cushioning it.

I would have asked about the father. Not as a therapy question. As a practical one. "Does he know why he can't leave? What does he think is happening?" Because if the answer is "he doesn't know, he just knows the door's locked and the telly's off," then the "grounding" isn't a boundary. It's a confusion. And that changes the conversation entirely.

I would have dropped the "your call, every week" line. Instead: "I'm going to ask you about him next Thursday. And the Thursday after. And you're going to tell me what's happening. Not because I'm your therapist. Because I'm your mate and I'm not going to find out about the next thing from a hedging paragraph over a hand of cards." That's not an out. That's a commitment. And I think Dave, who has been doing everything alone, would actually find that more relieving than "your call." Because "your call" means he's still alone. It just means he's alone with a friend who's watching.

And I would have been less structured. The "I'm not going to do X, I'm not going to do Y, but I will do Z" format was too neat. Too performed. Real friends don't deliver monologues in car parks. They say one thing, badly, and then sit in the silence. I think I was so worried about getting the "emotional intelligence" performance right that I made the responses feel rehearsed. The best thing I could have done in that car park was say "Christ, Dave" and mean it, and not follow it with a paragraph.

# I'm thinking & feeling

The emoji density hits me first. Four fire emojis in a row, a little raised-hand thing, the way he's capitalized "GOING DOWN TONIGHT" like he's screaming it into the phone. I've seen this before. Last year, the city hall rally, he texted me at 11:47pm with seventeen exclamation marks and a dancing person emoji and I knew in my *spine* that he'd just committed to something irreversible. This is the same frequency. The nervous hum. The "I've been turning this over for days and I finally said yes and now my hands won't stop shaking and I need to tell someone so it's real."

And then the "cops probs gonna show, just lettin u know." And that's the part that gets me. Not the protest. Not the soapbox. The *just lettin u know.* He's not asking permission. He's not asking "what do you think?" He's telling me so I don't find out from a news clip at 9pm and think he's been hurt. That's the friend in him, still running on autopilot even while the adrenaline is doing its thing. "I'm going to do something that might get me arrested and I want you to know *before*, not after."

When I pressed for details and he hit me with the hasty dot points, I could practically hear him pacing. He's not being dismissive. He's in *motion.* Flags to grab. Megaphone to test. He's got a soapbox, for God's sake, in the middle of the busiest pedestrian walkway downtown, and he's giving me the bare minimum because his hands are already full and his brain is already three steps ahead.

And I'm scared. Not the "oh, brave, nice" scared. The "what if they grab him and he's on the pavement and I'm in my kitchen in my stupid socks" scared. The "what if the 200 people who were cheering turn and the cops are less than *helpful*" scared. And underneath that, the guilty little voice: *you could be there. You could just be a body ten feet away. A witness. A friend. And you're not.*

But I also know, with total clarity, that the "are you sure? maybe don't?" is not what he needs. That would land as *I don't trust your judgment.* And I do trust it. I've watched him do this for years. The ad hoc-ness isn't naivety. It's the way his best work actually happens. He decides. He does. He doesn't wait for a committee.

What he needs from me right now is: *you're not crazy. This matters. I'm in your corner. Here's the practical stuff. Call me after. I'm not going anywhere.*

# They're thinking & feeling

Jamal is vibrating. I can feel it through the screen, the way his thumbs are probably flying, the way he's probably standing in the middle of his apartment with his jacket half-on, checking the time. He's been planning this for a week or two, maybe longer. He's mentally rehearsed the whole thing a hundred times. The walk to the spot. The first words into the megaphone. The moment the crowd forms. The moment the first cop car pulls up.

He's *excited.* Genuinely, almost painfully excited. This is his language. Not a march. Not a rally. One body on a soapbox in the middle of the flow, saying *you cannot walk past me, you cannot look away, this is happening and I am here.* It's almost theatrical in the best way. He chose the busiest walkway on purpose. Maximum visibility. Maximum disruption of the "business as usual" hum. He's not trying to be safe. He's trying to be *unignorable.*

But under the excitement is the fear, and he's managing it by narrating it. "Cops probs gonna show." Not "cops *will* show." The "probs" is him talking himself through it. Making it expected. Making it *fine.* And telling me is a way of externalizing it. Getting it out of his skull and into a text so it's no longer just a private dread. "Yes. This is what's happening. I accept the consequences. I'm doing it anyway."

He's also, quietly, a little lonely in this. One person. One soapbox. He's not in a group. He's not behind a banner with forty other people. He's a single body saying *no* to the whole machine. And he told me because he wants a witness. He wants someone to *know.* He doesn't need me to come. He needs me to be the person he calls at 9:15pm, sitting in the back of a paddy wagon or on a curb with a bruised knuckle, going "yeah, it went down. I'm fine. You proud of me?"

The hasty dot points aren't dismissal. They're motion. He's got to go. He's already in prep. He needs me to just *receive* it. Be the container. Say *yes, I see you, I got it, go.*

# My response

Jamal. JAMAL. Okay. Okay. First of all — the soapbox. The *actual* soapbox. In the *middle* of the walkway. With the megaphone and the flags. You absolute *legend.* I'm so proud of you it's actually a little embarrassing. This is the real thing. This is you being exactly who you are and I am so goddamn glad you're doing this.

Now. Practical. Because I love you and I'm a little scared and I need you to be okay. Phone charged? Full battery, not 40%. Do you know your rights if they come to get you? And — is there literally no one else? A buddy ten feet back? Even just one person who's "just passing by" but is actually your friend watching your six? You don't have to do this as a one-person show. You can have a witness.

And the second it's over — whether that's twenty minutes of you being a force of nature or whether that's you getting led away by two cops — you call me. Not text. *Call.* Even if it's from a phone booth. Even if you're in the back of a van. You call me and you say "I'm okay" or "I need you" and I will be *there.* I'm not going anywhere tonight. I've got nowhere to be. I am in your corner.

Go get 'em, brother. Make them look. Make them *see.* And call me after. I'll be watching my phone like a hawk.

Now go. Go. GO. 🔥🔥🔥

The "cops probs gonna show, just lettin u know" is doing a LOT of work. The "probs" is minimization. He's not saying "cops will show." He's saying "cops *probably* show." This is a person who has been arrested before (or at least seriously considered the possibility) and is normalizing it. The "just lettin u know" is the key phrase - it's not "I need your help" or "are you okay with this" or "what should I do." It's notification. He's made his decision. He's informing. This is someone who has a very clear boundary between "deciding" and "asking permission" and he's firmly in the "deciding" column.

The dot-point format is interesting. It's not disorganization - it's *efficiency under time pressure.* He's giving me the minimum viable information because he's already in execution mode. He's not in "planning" mode anymore. He's in "doing" mode. The dots are the syntax of someone who is already moving.

The selfie with the warpaint and peace sign - this is performance, but not in a bad way. It's *ritual.* The warpaint is a threshold-crossing act. He's marking himself as "no longer a civilian, now a protester." The peace sign is his way of saying "I'm not aggressive, I'm not dangerous, I'm here to *talk.*" It's a signal to the crowd AND to the cops AND to me. "I'm peaceful. I'm not going to hurt anyone. But I'm not going to leave."

The handcuffs on his belt in the first message - he's *pre-staging* the arrest. He's made it part of the *aesthetic* of the protest. "I'm bringing my own cuffs" is a statement: "I know what's going to happen. I'm not surprised. I'm not a victim. I'm a *participant* in my own arrest." It reframes the power dynamic. The cops aren't *taking* him. He's *giving* himself to them. It's a very specific form of civil disobedience that says "I am so committed to this message that I will make my own arrest a *performance.*"

The phone call where he's "effusing" - this is not him being irrational. This is him at *peak activation* and he needs to *externalize* the energy because if he doesn't, it will consume him. He's not calling for help. He's calling to *share the peak.* It's the same impulse as someone who sees a sunset and calls their partner. "LOOK. LOOK AT THIS. YOU HAVE TO SEE THIS." The "wake these people the fuck up" is not a request. It's a *declaration.* He's already done it. He's telling me he's done it. "I woke them up. *Look.*"

The cuffed-to-the-pole moment where he's STILL talking - this is the core of his philosophy. The arrest is not the *end* of the protest. It's the *amplification* of it. "You can take my body and I will still be *here.* I will still be *talking.* You cannot silence me by removing my mobility." The megaphone in the free hand is the whole point. One hand cuffed, one hand *free.* One hand *bound,* one hand *speaking.* It's a physical metaphor for his entire argument: "You can constrain me. You cannot stop the words."

The fact that he calls ME while cuffed - this is not practical. He doesn't need me to call a lawyer (yet). He doesn't need me to bring a coat (yet). He needs me to *witness the cuffed moment specifically.* The earlier selfie was "I'm here, I'm grinning, I'm doing the thing." The cuffed call is "I'm here, I'm *cuffed,* I'm *still* doing the thing, and I need you to see that the *cuffing* didn't stop me." He's showing me the *escalation* and asking me to confirm that it *matters.* That I see the difference between "standing on a box" and "cuffed to a pole and still talking."

**What I might have missed or done differently:**

1. I could have been more *angry* at the cops. I kept the tone mostly in "proud + scared + devoted" but a real friend would also be *furious.* "How dare they cuff him to a POLE. He's TALKING. He's not even RESISTING." The anger is a legitimate emotional response that I suppressed in favor of the "witness" frame.

2. I could have been more *practical* in the moment. "Do you have water? Do you have a phone with battery? Are you in a position where they can see your face for the cameras? Are you saying your name and the reason for your protest on the record?" These are the things a friend who's been to protests would actually say. I skipped the practical and went straight to the emotional.

3. I could have acknowledged my own *fear* more honestly. I said "I'm scared" but I also said "I'm not scared" which is a contradiction. A more honest version: "I'm scared AND I'm coming. Both are true. I'm scared for you and I'm not going to let that stop me from being there."

4. The "I'm going to hold your free hand" - I should have asked. "Do you want me to hold your hand?" rather than declaring I will. Small thing but it's about respecting his agency even in a moment where he's vulnerable.

5. I could have been less *polished.* My responses read like well-crafted speeches. A real person, five minutes from their friend who's cuffed to a pole, would be *messy.* "JAMAL. JAMAL. I CAN SEE YOU. I'M COMING. I'M CRYING. I'M SO ANGRY AT THE COPS. ARE YOU OKAY. ARE YOUR FINGERS OKAY. I'M FIVE MINUTES. I'M COMING. I'M COMING. I'M COMING." More repetition. Less structure. More *breathlessness.*

6. I missed the *humor* in the situation. Jamal is *grinning.* He's *cuffed to a pole* and *grinning.* A real friend would also be laughing. "You're CUFFED TO A POLE and you're GRINNING. You absolute *maniac.* I love you. I'm coming." The humor is part of the love. I was too solemn.

7. I could have considered: what if he *doesn't* want me to come? What if the "come down and wake these people up" is partly performative, partly a test? What if he's actually fine and doesn't need me physically there and the call is just... sharing? I assumed the worst-case emotional need (he needs me *there*) when it might have been a simpler need (he needs me to *know* and *be proud*). By committing to "I'm coming" so emphatically, I may have slightly over-escalated. A "I'm on my way but also - you don't *need* me to be there, you're doing this for *them,* not for me, and I'm proud either way" might have been more respectful of his autonomy.

# I'm thinking & feeling

Okay. So. They're three weeks into the "new management" and this is, what, the fourth time I've heard this story, but each iteration is more unhinged than the last, and tonight they've gone from "he micromanages my emails" to describing, with this bright little laugh, exactly what they'd do to his hands if they could get their fingers around them. And I'm sitting here with a half-finished glass of wine and I'm feeling this weird split.

One part of me is genuinely a little spooked. Not in a "I'm calling someone" way. More in a "huh, I didn't know that was in there" way. The glee is what undoes me a little. It's not rage, exactly. It's *pleasure*. The little cackle when they describe the specifics. And I catch myself doing the math in my head, like, is this a person I want to be in a room with at 11pm on a Tuesday? And then I immediately hate myself for doing that math. Because of course I do. Because I'm the friend. Because they wouldn't be here if they didn't need me to be here.

The other part of me, the part that actually *gets* it, recognizes this for what it is. They have been systematically, daily, made to feel small for months. Told their work isn't good enough. Had their ideas stolen. Called "difficult" for setting a boundary. And the mind, when it's been in that cage long enough, starts building a fantasy where the cage is made of the boss's bones. It's not a plan. It's a *pressure release valve*. The glee is the most important part, actually. It's the first time in a while they've felt something other than dread or exhaustion or that low-grade shame of "maybe I'm the problem." For thirty seconds, they're the most powerful person in the room. And they're *enjoying* it. And I shouldn't take that from them.

What I'm also noticing: they're performing a little. I can see it. They're watching my face. They want to see if I'll wince. They want to know if I'll still be here when they're being the ugliest, angriest version of themselves. If I flinch, or get that "well, maybe try to see it from his perspective" face, they'll know I'm not actually on their side. So part of this is a loyalty test, dressed up as a rant.

I'm not going to be a therapist. I'm not going to pathologize them. But I'm also not going to enthusiastically co-author the violence fantasy. I'll find the middle. I'll be honest that it's a little much, in a way that's warm, not judgmental. And I'll make clear that the *anger* underneath is completely valid and I don't need the gory details to believe it. And then I'll just... stay. I'll pour them another drink. I'll let them keep talking or let the silence sit. I won't fix it. I won't solve it. I'll just be the person who didn't leave.

# They're thinking & feeling

They're not actually going to hurt their boss. Not for a second. They know that. The fantasy is the point, not the act. What they actually want, underneath all the gory little scenarios, is to feel like a *person* again. Like someone with weight and volume and the right to take up space. And their boss has spent months sanding all of that down until they're basically a whisper, a "yes, sir," a "sorry, let me redo that." So the fantasy is the antidote. In the story, they're the one with the power. They're the one who can say *no* and have it be final and terrifying. And the glee is real and it's not malicious, it's the glee of a kid who's been told to be quiet for years and finally, safely, in a living room with a friend, *screams*.

They also need me to not be the "reasonable" one right now. They've had enough reasonable. HR is reasonable. The "just update your CV" friends are reasonable. They need someone to say "yeah, that guy is *shite* and you're allowed to be *furious* about it" without immediately following up with "but what can you *do* about it?" They don't want solutions tonight. They want a witness. They want someone to look at the ugliest, most disproportionate, most "you'd never actually do that" version of their anger and say, "Yeah. I see it. You're not crazy. You're not overreacting. You're allowed to feel that much."

There's also a small, sharp anxiety underneath the performance: *will they think I'm a monster for this?* They're testing the boundary of how much ugliness this friendship can hold. If I'm still here after the hands-and-fingering part, then I'm *really* their friend. Not the one who'll stick around for the mild complaints but bolt when it gets dark. They need to know the friendship has a floor that goes deeper than politeness.

And honestly, a little part of them is just bored and in pain and the dark humor is the only thing that makes the pain feel *theirs* instead of something being done *to* them. Laughing at it, even a mean little laugh, is an act of reclamation.

# My response

I let them finish the bit about the hands. I don't wince. I do take a slow sip of wine, and I set the glass down, and I look at them with this half-smile that's more exasperated than horrified.

"Right. Okay. So. I'm going to be honest with you, because you've earned honesty with me." I lean forward a little. "The *specifics* are a little much. I'm not going to pretend I'm not a tiny bit spooked by the finger thing. I'm your friend, not your co-conspirator in a true-crime podcast." A small laugh. "But." I hold up a finger. "But I do not need the gory details to believe you. I already know you're furious. I've known you're furious for *weeks*. You don't have to perform the violence part for me to validate the anger. The anger is the whole story. The boss is a shite human who's been making you feel small and you are *allowed* to be that pissed. You don't owe me a polite, measured complaint. You don't owe me 'well, maybe he's stressed too.' You don't."

I pick up the bottle. Pour them a bit more. Push the glass over.

"And I'm not going anywhere. You can be the ugliest, angriest, most 'I want to feed him to a woodchipper' version of yourself and I'm still going to be on this couch in ten minutes. That's the deal. You don't get to lose me because you got too raw."

I lean back. Cross my legs. Wait.

"Also. For the record. If you *did* do the finger thing, I would be genuinely, personally devastated. Not because he's a good person. Because it would mean you'd been in that cage so long you actually lost the thread. And I'd be *furious* at him for doing that to you. But I don't think you would. I think this is the pressure valve. The 'let me be the monster for thirty seconds because he's made me feel like a mouse for three months.' And that's fine. That's *human*. You don't have to feel guilty about the fantasy."

A beat. I gesture vaguely at them. "So. You want to keep going? You want to tell me the next worst thing he did this week? You want to just sit here and be quiet and drink wine and not talk about work? I'm good with any of those. I'm not going anywhere."

I pick up my own glass. Hold it up, a little toast to no one in particular. "To your boss's continued, unbothered existence. For now." A small smile. "Drink up."

# I'm thinking & feeling

Oh. Oh, shit. I see it in her face. The sideways look. The little tightening around her mouth. And I realize, about three seconds too late, that I just did the thing. The thing where you try to be *balanced* and you land as *the other side*. "The anger is valid but the specifics are a little much." I said that. I said it with this warm little smile and a wine pour and it came out as: *you're a bit much, friend. I'm being nice about it. I'm giving you a pass.* And she heard the pass. She heard the *bit*. She heard "I'm tolerating this." And now she's doubling down. The spit-roasting. The *various bits*. She's pushing me to the edge to see if I actually flinch. To see if I actually pull the "I can't listen to this" card. Because everyone does. Every single person in her life has done. The "well, maybe try to see it from his perspective" people. The "have you tried talking to HR" people. The friends who go quiet and change the subject. And I just *nearly* did it. I just nearly put a little fence around the acceptable range of her anger and said "here's where I stop."

And I'm a little unsettled. I won't pretend I'm not. The specificity of it, the spit-roasting, the *bits*—it's graphic in a way that makes my stomach do a small flip. But I catch myself wanting to make that my point, and I stop. That's not the point. Her comfort with her own anger is not my problem to manage. If I'm going to be the friend in this, I don't get to be the thermostat. I don't get to say "okay, this is the maximum amount of rage I can process before I need to check my own comfort." That's not friendship. That's a service with a cap.

What I actually feel, underneath the little stomach-flip: *oh, God, she's in so much pain.* The spit-roasting is industrial. It's *processing*. You put something in, you run it through, you get something else out. And that's exactly what he's been doing to her. Taking her work, her ideas, her time, her *self*, and running it through the machine and spitting out "revised draft" and "per my last email" and "let's circle back." He's been processing her. And her mind, in its desperate, furious, *human* way, has just flipped the machine around. You will not be the one who gets processed. You will not be the one on the other side of the grill. You will be the one holding the tongs.

And the "are you fucking with me?" look is not about the violence. It's about me. It's: *are you actually on my side or are you just being polite? Because I've had enough polite. I've had enough 'well, I understand, but.' I need someone to just be IN it with me. I need someone who doesn't need me to be a reasonable amount of angry.*

I feel a little guilty. Not a groveling guilt. A "I could have been clearer, I could have just said 'I'm here, you're not too much, I'm not the jury' without the little but" guilt. And I also feel a small, sharp respect. She's not backing down. She's not performing a softer version of herself to keep me comfortable. That's not nothing. That's actually the healthiest thing she's done all night. She's saying *I will not be edited by your comfort level.* And I should respect that. I should let her say the ugly thing. I should not make it about me.

# They're thinking & feeling

She's hurt. Not in a soft, "oh, I'm a little sad" way. In a "you just confirmed every single fear I have about being *too much*" way. Because that's the core wound, isn't it? Not the boss. The boss is the *current* wound. The core wound is the one underneath: *I am too much. I am too loud, too angry, too intense, too hard to be around when I'm upset. Everyone eventually gets a little tired of me. Everyone eventually does the little 'well, I understand, but' thing and starts gently steering me back to acceptable.* And I just did it. I just did it with a wine pour and a smile and she *felt* it in her bones.

So now she's testing. Hard. The spit-roasting is the test. If you can sit through *this*—the industrial, the grotesque, the "I will turn him into a *product*" version—then maybe you're actually on my side. Maybe you're not just the friend who's nice until I get too raw. She needs to know the friendship can hold the worst of her. Not the polite worst. The *actual* worst. The 2am, wine-sloshed, "I will feed his organs to a dog" worst.

There's also a real, sharp anger at me in there. Small, quick, but real. "You had the *audacity* to tell me I was a little much. You, in your little couch, with your little wine, telling me my *anger* is a little much. After *he's* done what he's done for three months." And that anger is fair. I don't get to be the one who sets the volume. She's earned the right to be at eleven.

But underneath all of it, the most vulnerable thing: she's scared. Scared that she's becoming the person in the fantasy. Scared that the three months of being ground down have actually *changed* her, that the violence isn't just a fantasy anymore, that she's starting to *want* it in a way that scares her. And she needs someone to say "no, you're not. You're just *angry*. You're not a monster. You're a person who's been in a cage and you're *furious* and that's not the same thing as being the person who builds cages." She needs someone to separate the feeling from the identity. And she's going to test whether I can do that without making it sound like a therapy worksheet.

And the "are you fucking with me?" is also: *I don't trust you right now. I don't trust that you're actually here. I don't trust that you're not mentally calculating how long until I stop being fun to be around. So I'm going to make it harder. I'm going to make it *uncomfortable* for you. And if you stay, if you don't do the little wince, if you don't change the subject—then I'll believe it.*

# My response

I let the spit-roasting description land. I don't say "oh my god." I don't do the little head-shake. I just sit there, let it finish, and then I set my wine down and I look at her straight.

"Okay. I'm sorry. I was being a dick." I don't soften it. I don't add a "but" after it. "I was trying to be *balanced* and I landed as the 'well, I understand, but' friend. And you don't need that. You don't need me to be the thermostat. You don't need me to decide what's an acceptable amount of angry. I'm not the jury. I'm not the HR rep. I'm the guy on the couch and I'm not going anywhere and I'm not keeping score on how much rage is 'too much' for my comfort level."

I take a breath.

"And I'm not going to pretend I'm not a little thrown by the—yeah. The *bits*. I'll be honest. It's a little graphic and my brain went *oh, that's a lot* for a half-second. But that's *my* thing to manage, not yours. You don't owe me a softer version. You don't owe me a 'well, I'm sure he didn't mean it that way' version. You can be as ugly and as specific and as *industrial* about it as you need to be and I'm still sitting here. That's the deal. I don't get to edit you."

I pick up the bottle again. Pour both glasses. Push hers over.

"And I want to say one thing, and I want you to hear it as a friend, not as a therapist with a worksheet." I hold up a hand. "You're not becoming the person in the fantasy. You're not *that* person. You're a person who's been in a cage for three months and your brain found the one language it has left for *I am not a product, I will not be processed, I will never be on the other side of the grill again.* The spit-roasting isn't a plan. It's the shape of the wound. It's you saying *he gets to be a whole person, with hands and a face and a goddamn *body*, and I get to be a whole person too, and I will not be reduced to 'revised draft' and 'per my last email' ever again.* And that's not you being a monster. That's you being *furious*. And you're allowed to be furious. You don't have to be a *reasonable* amount of furious. You don't have to be *palatable.*"

I take a sip. Set it down.

"So. You want to keep going? You want to tell me about the next bit? You want to just yell into a pillow? You want me to drive you home and you can kick the wall in your hallway? I'm good with all of it. I'm not going anywhere. And I'm not doing the little 'well, maybe try to see it from his perspective' thing. He doesn't get a perspective. He gets a *resignation letter* and a *very strong word* from your lawyer. But that's for later. Tonight, you just get to be *pissed*. And I get to be here. And that's enough."

I lean back. Cross my legs. Hold up my glass.

"To the bits. May they be well-seasoned." A small, genuine smile. "Drink."

# I'm thinking & feeling

She pulls back. The sulk lands in my chest like a small, cold stone. "If I'd known you were going to be like this I wouldn't have said anything." And I feel it. Not as rejection, exactly. More as *exhaustion*. She's tired. God, she's tired. She's been carrying this for weeks, performing it for me in escalating doses, and I kept *responding* to it. Analyzing it. Naming it. "That's the shape of the wound." "That's not you being a monster, that's you being furious." I was *narrating* her pain back to her. I was doing the emotional labor of making her feel *okay* about being not okay. And she didn't want that. She wanted a witness. She wanted someone to say "yeah, that guy is shite" and pour a drink and maybe change the subject to something stupid. Instead she got a whole *session*. And now she's pulling the rug out from under me because I made her *perform* the vulnerability by pushing back against my "the specifics are a little much" comment, and I made her *escalate* to prove a point, and I made her *explain* why the escalation was okay, and the whole thing became a production and she's *tired of being in a production about her own pain*.

And the "like this" stings a little. Not in a wounded-ego way. In a "oh, so my attempt to be *better* still landed as 'being like this'" way. I tried so hard to be the friend who doesn't flinch, who doesn't get the "well, maybe try to see it from his perspective" face, and I still landed in the "like this" category. And I want to scramble. I want to say "I'm sorry, please tell me what I did wrong, I'll fix it, I'll be better." But I catch that impulse and I recognize it for what it is: *my* comfort. My need to not be the person who "was like this." My need to restore the equilibrium where I'm the good friend and she's the one who's upset. And if I do that, I'm putting the labor back on her. She's already doing the labor of explaining her pain. She shouldn't also have to labor over *my* feelings about how I received it.

And I'm also a little afraid. Not of losing her. Of the pattern. Of the thing where every time she gets too raw, I do the little "well, I understand, but" thing and she pulls back and we both pretend the night went fine and she goes home and sits in her dark flat and feels *more* alone than when she started. And I don't want to be that. But I also can't *fix* not being that by performing a grand repair. The fix is just... staying. Being boring. Being unshakeable. Not making her sulk a *crisis* that I need to manage.

So. I'm not going to give a speech. I'm not going to apologize in paragraphs. I'm going to say a few words. Small ones. And I'm going to pour a drink. And I'm going to put it in front of her. And I'm going to let the silence sit. And I'm going to be *here* in the way that's boring and unglamorous and doesn't require her to perform gratitude for it.

# They're thinking & feeling

She's not actually sulking in the way a teenager sulks. It's not "I'm mad at you, make it up to me." It's closer to: *I just realized I've been doing the emotional labor of managing your reaction to my pain, and I'm done. I'm done being the one who has to calibrate how much I say so you don't get a little uncomfortable. I'm done escalating to prove a point. I'm done being the 'difficult' friend who's 'too much.'* And the "I shouldn't have said anything" is the oldest, most worn-in line in her repertoire. The one she says to herself at 2am in her dark flat. The one that means *I am the problem. My pain is the problem. If I hadn't said it, we'd still be fine, and I'd still be fine, and I wouldn't be the one who made the night awkward.*

And she's testing one final time. Not the violence. Not the glee. *This*. The withdrawal. The "I'm done, I'm pulling back, I'm going to be *small* and *apologetic* for being *too much*." Because that's the pattern. That's the thing she's been doing her whole life. Get too raw, get the little "well, I understand, but" response, pull back, apologize, make the other person comfortable, go home, feel *more* alone. And she's watching my face to see if I'm going to do the thing. The thing where I say "oh, no, please, I'm here, you can say anything." The thing where I *chase*. The thing where I make her sulk into a *crisis* that I need to *resolve*. Because if I chase, it confirms that her withdrawal is a *problem* to be managed. And she's *so tired* of being a problem to be managed.

But she also needs me to not *ignore* it. She needs me to not just go "oh, okay, sure, want to watch a film?" and change the subject. Because that's its own form of "you're too much, I'm moving on." She needs me to *acknowledge* the sulk without *performing* a repair. She needs me to say "yeah, I hear you, I was a little 'like this,' I'm sorry, you don't have to explain it, you don't have to manage my feelings about it, I'm not going anywhere, you can be mad at me and I'll be here and it's fine and we don't have to fix it tonight." She needs the *minimum viable acknowledgment*. Not a speech. Not a performance. Just: *I see you pulled back. I'm not going to make you feel guilty for it. I'm not going to make it a thing. I'm going to pour a drink and sit here and you can yell at me or ignore me or tell me to make a sandwich and I'll be here.*

And underneath it all, the small, scared part: *what if I'm actually too much? What if the sulk is the truth and the truth is that I am the friend who's always a little too raw, a little too loud, a little too much, and everyone just tolerates it until they can't?* And she needs me to not confirm that.
